opus-5.5.text:
I think the most urgent problem is data. Really, the lack of data.

Look at what happened with large language models. They worked because we had the internet, trillions of tokens of text that humans had already written down. Robotics has nothing like that. There's no internet of robot actions. Every bit of data about how a robot should move its arm, grasp a cup, or recover when something slips has to be collected physically, on real hardware, in real time. It's slow, expensive, and it doesn't scale the way text or images do.

That's the main bottleneck. We have increasingly capable models, vision-language-action models, foundation models that can reason about the world, but they're starved for the kind of embodied, physical interaction data they need to generalize. A model can tell you how to fold a shirt, but actually doing it, with the contact, deformation, and tiny corrections, requires a different kind of experience.

So the question the whole field is working on is: how do we get enough data? There are a few paths. One is simulation, which is a big part of my own background. In simulation you can run thousands of robots in parallel, faster than real time, and that has worked very well for locomotion. We can now train legged robots entirely in sim and deploy them in the real world. But for manipulation, especially rich contact and deformable objects, the sim-to-real gap is still significant. Another path is learning from human videos, since there's a huge amount of humans doing things on video, but there's an embodiment gap: a human hand isn't a robot gripper, and video doesn't directly give you forces or actions. And then there's scaling real-world data collection with teleoperation and fleets of robots, which works but is costly.

I don't think any single one of these will be the answer. It'll likely be a combination: pretraining on internet-scale video and language for common sense and semantics, simulation for scale and safe exploration, and a smaller amount of high-quality real robot data to ground it all.

Closely tied to that is generalization and reliability. Today, many impressive robot demos work maybe 80 or 90 percent of the time in a fairly controlled setting. But for a robot to be useful in a home or a factory, you need something like 99.9 percent, in environments it's never seen before. Closing that gap from "works in the demo" to "works every day in the real world" is, I think, the real challenge, and fundamentally it comes back to data and how we use it.

r001.rationale: The response says no single data source or approach will be the answer, but it does not state that solving one problem is insufficient to make robots work.

r002.rationale: It identifies lack of data as the most urgent problem and mentions high-quality real-robot data as one ingredient, but does not identify obtaining high-quality data itself as potentially the most urgent problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. If I had to name one thing, I'd say it's data. The reason language models took off is that there was essentially an internet's worth of text to learn from. Robotics has nothing like that. Every robot has a different body, different sensors, different actuators, and the data we collect from one often doesn't transfer to another. So the field is stuck in this loop where you collect a small dataset for one task on one robot, train a policy, and then start over for the next.

The question I spend most of my time on is how to break out of that loop. Simulation is one answer, and I'm a big believer in it. You can generate enormous amounts of experience very cheaply, and with reinforcement learning you can discover behaviors that nobody knew how to program by hand, like getting a quadruped to recover from a fall or walk on ice. But the simulation-to-real gap is still there, and closing it takes real engineering judgment, not just more compute.

The other answer is to borrow what the language and vision models already know. A model that has read the whole internet understands a great deal about objects, tasks, and physical common sense. If you can connect that knowledge to a robot's low-level control, you get a robot that can take an instruction like "clear the table" and actually decompose it into something it can execute. We've seen early versions of that work, and I think it's where a lot of the leverage is.

So if I zoom out, the urgent problem is building the data flywheel. Once robots can learn from simulation, from internet knowledge, and from their own deployments at scale, progress will compound the way it has for language. Until then, we're hand-crafting one robot at a time, and that's just too slow.

r001.rationale: The response describes data collection and transfer challenges across tasks and robots, but does not state that solving one problem is insufficient to make robots work.

r002.rationale: The response calls data the urgent problem, but does not identify obtaining high-quality data; it discusses data volume, scale, and transfer instead.

astra-6.text:
I think the most urgent problem is making robots reliable in the real world. We can build a robot that performs a task beautifully in a demonstration, but can it do that task thousands of times, when the environment changes or something unexpected happens? That’s still very difficult.

A big part of this is generalization. We can’t anticipate every situation a robot will encounter and program a response for it. Robots need to learn from experience, adapt to new situations, and recover from mistakes safely. I think closing that gap between a successful demonstration and dependable everyday operation is what will make robots truly useful.

r001.rationale: It says a robot’s successful demonstration is not enough; reliable operation across repeated tasks, changing environments, and unexpected events is still needed.

r002.rationale: The response discusses reliability, generalization, and learning from experience, but does not identify obtaining high-quality data as a potentially urgent problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most urgent problem is generalization. We can build robots that perform a specific task very well in a controlled environment, but when you put them in a new home or a new workplace, they often struggle. The lighting changes, an object is in a different place, or something unexpected happens.

So the challenge is: how do we get robots to learn skills that transfer to new situations, and to recover when things go wrong? That also means making them safe and reliable around people. A successful demonstration is exciting, but a useful robot needs to work consistently, day after day.

r001.rationale: The response explains that performing one specific task well in a controlled environment is insufficient: robots must transfer skills to new situations and work consistently.

r002.rationale: The response identifies generalization, recovery, safety, and reliability as challenges, but does not identify obtaining high-quality data as a potentially urgent problem.
